Alaska.Ai — Anchorage Desk Draft

2026-09-24 · branch claude/linkedin-desk-2026-09-24

Copy this for LinkedIn

Ben Shier, the University of Alaska’s Chief Information Technology Officer, has put a draft AI policy before the Board of Regents. If approved in November, UAA and every other UA campus must adopt an AI plan.

Shier leads the UA System Office of Information Technology and is a former UAA Chief Information Officer. If adopted, the policy would require UAA, the campus where he was once CIO, to write its own AI plan.

According to KTOO, Shier presented the draft at the September regents meeting at UAS in Juneau, first reported Sept. 16. Its guiding principles are to avoid replacing human talent, keep data secure, and use AI to widen access to education services. He framed the core governance problem as two questions. “How do you ensure data privacy and protection? How do you provide monitoring?”

The regents now have a real choice to make. AI adoption can stay with campuses, departments and faculty under existing data rules, or a top-down framework can require UAA, UAF and UAS to each produce a plan for students, faculty and staff.

The direction is right. A 2025 Inside Higher Ed survey cited by KTOO found about 85% of college students use generative AI in coursework, so use is already ahead of policy.

UA isn’t starting from zero either. OIT’s Generative AI Security Standard, effective January 2025, already bars Internal and Restricted data, such as FERPA and HIPAA data, from unapproved generative AI tools. The draft moves UA from a data-handling rule to an institutional expectation. Setting guardrails before use spreads further is the correct order of operations.

The honest gap is process, and Shier named it himself. He said the draft came together over the summer without enough faculty and student feedback, and that UA can’t currently control and track every use of AI. Regent Christine Ressler raised concerns about data security capabilities, according to KTOO. That’s a reason for care, not alarm. The risk is a November vote that adopts principles before UA can enforce them. For UAA, the useful test is whether the campus plan requirement comes with the resources to carry it out.

Next come fall student listening sessions and online surveys, which had no dates as of Sept. 16. After that, leadership plans to bring a finalized draft for approval at the November 2026 regents meeting. The thing to watch is whether faculty and student input visibly changes the final text, and whether the monitoring question Shier posed gets a concrete answer before the vote.

Should the regents approve the framework in November as drafted, or hold it until faculty input and a monitoring plan are in hand?

#AlaskaAI #AIPolicy #WorkforceDevelopment

Editor note:
Subject this cycle: Ben Shier, CITO of the University of Alaska System, and the draft system-wide AI policy he presented to the Board of Regents (reported Sept. 16, 2026). Role slot RESEARCH. Scored 8.64/10 against the desk rubric, all 9 hard-fail checks passed.

CAVEATS TO READ BEFORE POSTING
1) Single reporting line. The two news sources are ONE story by Jamie Diep (KTOO), syndicated by Alaska Public Media. The validator wrongly called them separate bylines; I caught that during re-verification. Both are independent of UA, so the rubric's independence rule holds, but there's no second newsroom. No Juneau Empire, Alaska Beacon, or BOR agenda/minutes coverage turned up (UA BoardDocs is only posted through June 2026). The UA OIT Generative AI Security Standard page is added as context from UA itself, not as independent corroboration.
2) The Anchorage tie is bowl-impact, not residency. Shier is Fairbanks-based UA System staff and a former UAA CIO. The meeting was at UAS in Juneau. The post's tie is that the policy would require UAA to write an AI plan.
3) This is a DRAFT. The binding vote is at the November 2026 regents meeting.
4) Only one Shier quote was confirmed word for word, and it's the only one used. Regent Christine Ressler's concern is paraphrased, not quoted.

EDIT AND SCORE TRAIL
Editor cycle 1 (revise): cut a speculative line about Shier "asking" UAA to write its plan, and removed "Shier's draft/framework" possessives (sources say he presented the draft, not that he wrote it). Editor cycle 2: body cleared; the headline was changed to "UAA Would Write a Plan" so it doesn't state the obligation as fact. The scorer's only note was readability (two 6-7 sentence paragraphs). I split both after scoring without changing any words.

DROPPED CANDIDATES (in brief)
Daniel Volland and Mayor Suzanne LaFrance (the AO 2026-108 surveillance ordinance, postponed Sept. 15 to Oct. 20) both held the spine. They were set aside only because this would be the fifth surveillance cycle in seven issues. The Oct. 20 vote is a strong next-week candidate. Aaron Dotson (AI@UAA), Masoumeh Heidari (UAA EEG lab) and Nathan Reed (Northrim/Narmi) failed independent corroboration. Naji Kjoury (Alaska Communications CEO hire) fell outside the window. Louis Wolfson (DeepGreen) doesn't own the FERC act and has no Anchorage tie. The founders and operators slices were thin this week.

RUN DEVIATIONS
- This run followed the repo's current prompts/desk_instructions.md for the image and email: bespoke alaska-ai-artwork art, with the permanent image link pinned to the exact commit. The scheduled prompt still says to use the old alaska-ai-brief template, and that section is out of date. The scheduled prompt's 60-day window and 21-day subject rule were used for editorial (the repo file still says 30 days / 12 issues). Worth reconciling the two prompt versions.
- Artwork: "trail markers behind the trail" engraving (style engraving_trail, hue blue, diagonal_thrust). 6 eval iterations, final 8.53 (the 8.5 floor), weakest dimension focal. art_kit.field() with opensimplex took about 54 seconds per call in this container, so the script uses a local numpy noise instead. That's worth a kit fix.
- No window broadening, no subagent stalls, no conflict screen triggered.
